items.followUp: Why does ice have a lower density than liquid water?

rubric.why: Identifies the structure formed in ice that explains its lower density.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonds arrange water molecules in ice into an open, expanded structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking hydrogen bonding in ice to an open or expanded structure.

rubric.why: States the density difference and connects it to floating.
rubric.description: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats on water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice is less dense than liquid water and floats as a result.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonds arrange water molecules in ice into an open, expanded structure.
This makes ice less dense than liquid water, so it floats on water.

items.followUp: What conditions are required for dynamic equilibrium in a reversible reaction?

rubric.why: Identifies the opposing reactions and the equal rates required at dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: In a reversible reaction, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both reactions continue in a reversible reaction at equal rates.

rubric.why: States the consequence of the equal forward and reverse rates.
rubric.description: The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, so there is no overall change.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that concentrations remain constant or that there is no overall change.

modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
As a result, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

items.followUp: What keeps the particles of a colloid from settling out quickly?

rubric.why: Describes the small size of colloidal particles and their persistence in dispersion.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles are very small and remain dispersed instead of settling under gravity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the small particles remain dispersed or do not settle.

rubric.why: Gives a mechanism that helps keep colloidal particles dispersed.
rubric.description: Continuous Brownian motion, or repulsion between like charges, helps keep the colloid stable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Brownian motion or repulsion between like-charged particles.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles are very small and remain dispersed instead of settling under gravity.
Their continuous Brownian motion, and often repulsion between like charges, helps keep the colloid stable.

items.followUp: Give five differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Contrasts the chemical combination and fixed composition of a compound with the physical mixing and variable composition of a mixture.
rubric.description: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains substances physically mixed in variable proportions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both parts of this contrast.

rubric.why: Contrasts the properties of a compound with those of its components in a mixture.
rubric.description: A compound has properties different from its constituent elements; substances in a mixture retain their own properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both parts of this property contrast.

rubric.why: Contrasts how compounds and mixtures are separated.
rubric.description: The elements of a compound are separated by chemical methods; mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting chemical and physical separation methods.

rubric.why: Contrasts the fixed melting and boiling points of a pure compound with the range typical of a mixture.
rubric.description: A pure compound has definite melting and boiling points; a mixture generally melts or boils over a range.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating this contrast in melting and boiling behaviour.

rubric.why: Contrasts a compound's homogeneous nature with the fact that a mixture may be heterogeneous.
rubric.description: A compound is homogeneous; a mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating this contrast.

modelAnswer: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains substances physically mixed in variable proportions.
A compound has properties different from its constituent elements; the substances in a mixture retain their own properties.
The elements of a compound are separated by chemical methods; mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
A pure compound has definite melting and boiling points; a mixture generally melts or boils over a range.
A compound is homogeneous; a mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

items.followUp: Write four properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Identifies the charge and nature of canal rays.
rubric.description: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles, or positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying canal rays as positively charged particles or positive ions.

rubric.why: States the path followed by canal rays.
rubric.description: Canal rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that canal rays travel in straight lines.

rubric.why: Describes the deflection of canal rays in fields or relative to cathode rays.
rubric.description: Canal rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields in the direction expected for positive charges, opposite to cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct electric-field or magnetic-field deflection property, or for stating that their deflection is opposite to that of cathode rays.

rubric.why: States that the nature of canal-ray particles depends on the gas in the tube.
rubric.description: The particles and their mass-to-charge ratio depend on the gas present in the discharge tube.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles or mass-to-charge ratio depend on the gas used.

modelAnswer: Canal rays consist of positively charged particles, or positive ions.
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields in the direction expected for positive charges, opposite to cathode rays.
Their particles, and their mass-to-charge ratio, depend on the gas present in the discharge tube.

items.followUp: Describe single, double and triple covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: States the defining feature of covalent bonding.
rubric.description: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining covalent bonding as sharing electron pairs.

rubric.why: Defines a single covalent bond and gives the model's example.
rubric.description: A single covalent bond has one shared pair; H₂ is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a single bond has one shared pair and giving H₂ as an example.

rubric.why: Defines a double covalent bond and gives the model's example.
rubric.description: A double covalent bond has two shared pairs; O₂ is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a double bond has two shared pairs and giving O₂ as an example.

rubric.why: Defines a triple covalent bond and gives the model's example.
rubric.description: A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs; N₂ is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a triple bond has three shared pairs and giving N₂ as an example.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share electron pairs.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Define an unsaturated solution and describe how to prepare one.

rubric.why: Defines saturation in terms of the maximum amount of solute that dissolves under stated conditions.
rubric.description: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the maximum-solute definition, including the solvent amount and temperature condition.

rubric.why: Gives the initial steps for preparing the solution.
rubric.description: Measure the solvent and add the solute gradually while stirring.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing measured solvent and gradual addition of solute while stirring.

rubric.why: States how to identify the saturation point during preparation.
rubric.description: Continue until no more solute dissolves; any excess remains undissolved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that no more solute dissolves or that excess solute remains undissolved.

rubric.why: Confirms the condition under which the prepared solution is saturated.
rubric.description: The solution is then saturated at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the resulting solution as saturated at the stated temperature.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
Measure the solvent and add the solute gradually while stirring.
Continue until no more solute dissolves; any excess remains undissolved.
The solution is then saturated at that temperature.
